prompt: A service gets 50 million requests a day, spread evenly. About how many requests per second is that?
why: A day has 86,400 seconds (round it to 100,000 for speed). 50,000,000 / 86,400 ≈ 580.

prompt: How much memory do 1 billion 64-bit integers take, with no overhead?
why: 64 bits = 8 bytes. 8 × 10^9 bytes = 8 GB.

prompt: 200 million daily users each post 2 messages a day of about 300 bytes. How much raw text is stored per year?
why: 200M × 2 × 300 B = 120 GB a day. × 365 ≈ 43.8 TB a year, before replicas, indexes and media.

prompt: How many seconds are in a (non-leap) year?
How long does it take to send 1 TB over a fully used 1 Gbps link?
why: 1 TB = 8 × 10^12 bits. At 10^9 bits per second that is 8,000 seconds ≈ 133 minutes. Remember bytes vs bits: a factor of 8.

prompt: How big is one uncompressed 1920×1080 frame at 24-bit colour?
why: 1920 × 1080 pixels × 3 bytes = 6,220,800 bytes ≈ 6.2 MB.

prompt: How much space does one hour of uncompressed 1080p video at 30 frames per second take (24-bit colour)?
why: 6.22 MB per frame × 30 × 3,600 ≈ 672 GB. That is why video is always compressed, usually by 100x or more.

prompt: How much memory do 10 million UUIDs take as raw 16-byte values?
why: 10^7 × 16 bytes = 160 MB. Stored as 36-character strings in a typical runtime it is several times more.

prompt: Each request takes 20 ms of CPU on one core. A server has 16 cores. What is its maximum throughput if CPU is the only limit?
why: One core does 1000 / 20 = 50 requests a second. 16 cores give 800. Plan to run well below that at peak.

prompt: Users upload 1 million images a day, 2 MB each on average. How much storage is that per year?
why: 1M × 2 MB = 2 TB a day. × 365 = 730 TB, before thumbnails and replication.

prompt: 10,000 people watch video at the same time, each at 5 Mbps. What total outbound bandwidth is that?
why: 10^4 × 5 × 10^6 bits/s = 5 × 10^10 = 50 Gbps. This is why video goes through a CDN.

prompt: How long does reading 1 GB sequentially take from an SSD that reads 500 MB per second?
why: 1,000 MB / 500 MB per second = 2 seconds.

prompt: A cache holds 100 million entries of about 100 bytes each (key plus value). How much memory is that, ignoring overhead?
why: 10^8 × 100 bytes = 10^10 bytes = 10 GB. Real overhead per entry often doubles it.

prompt: A service handles 2,000 requests a second all day and writes a 1 KB log line per request. How many logs does it write per day?
10 million users each open the app 10 times a day. Peak traffic is twice the daily average. What is the peak in requests per second (one request per open)?
why: 10^8 opens / 86,400 s ≈ 1,157 a second on average. Twice that ≈ 2,300 at peak.

prompt: How many distinct 7-character codes can you make from the 62 characters a-z, A-Z and 0-9?
why: 62^7 ≈ 3.5 × 10^12. That is why URL shorteners can use 7 characters for trillions of links.

prompt: An unsigned 32-bit counter increments 1,000 times a second. How long until it overflows?
why: 2^32 ≈ 4.29 × 10^9. Divided by 1,000 per second is 4.29 million seconds ≈ 49.7 days, a famous real-world uptime bug.

prompt: How many milliseconds are in one day?
why: 86,400 seconds × 1,000 = 86.4 million.

prompt: A table has 2 billion rows of about 500 bytes each. How big is the raw data?
why: 2 × 10^9 × 500 = 10^12 bytes = 1 TB, before indexes.

prompt: You must send 1 million emails and your provider allows 50 per second. How long does the full send take?
why: 10^6 / 50 = 20,000 seconds ≈ 5.6 hours. Queue it and show progress instead of blocking.

prompt: The current Unix time in milliseconds is about 1.8 × 10^12. How many bits do you need to store it?
why: 2^40 ≈ 1.1 × 10^12 is too small and 2^41 ≈ 2.2 × 10^12 fits, so 41 bits. That is why snowflake-style IDs give the timestamp 41 bits.

prompt: A chat server keeps 1 million open WebSocket connections, each using about 20 KB of memory. How much memory is that?
why: 10^6 × 20 KB = 2 × 10^10 bytes = 20 GB, which is why connection servers are tuned for per-connection memory.
